content: Vitamin A deficiency is prevalent in developing countries but is rarely observed in developed nations. Each year, approximately 250,000 to 500,000 malnourished children in the developing world lose their vision due to a lack of vitamin A. One of the earliest clinical manifestations of vitamin A deficiency is night blindness. This deficiency contributes to blindness by causing severe dryness of the cornea and by damaging both the retina and the cornea. Additionally, vitamin A deficiency impairs the immune system, reducing the body’s ability to combat infections. In regions where children are not routinely immunized, infectious diseases such as measles exhibit significantly higher mortality rates. As highlighted by Dr. Alfred Sommer, even mild or subclinical vitamin A deficiency can pose serious health risks. It can increase the likelihood of respiratory and diarrheal infections in children, slow their growth rate, hinder bone development, and reduce their chances of surviving severe illnesses. Beyond dietary insufficiency, other factors can contribute to vitamin A deficiency. For instance, iron deficiency can interfere with the body’s ability to absorb vitamin A. Excessive alcohol consumption can deplete vitamin A stores, and a liver under stress from alcohol may become more vulnerable to vitamin A toxicity. Individuals who consume large amounts of alcohol are advised to consult a healthcare professional before taking vitamin A supplements. Treatment for vitamin A deficiency can be administered through both oral and injectable forms, typically in the form of vitamin A palmitate.
